nodes.label: Adversarial review verdicts (C1 FIX, C2 KILL, C3 FIX)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: 13 web lookups plus one direct download of the organizers' dump. The three failures are on three different axes — prior art (C1), data (C2), demand (C3) — and none of them is where the generating pass was looking. All three pass the reduction test: HMAC mint + fingerprint ledger, DOI/ISBN/HTTP resolution, and minhash + LSH are classic model-free computer science.

nodes.label: Duke canary paper (arXiv:2605.13706) — Identifying AI Web Scrapers Using Canary Tokens
nodes.author: Seiden, Ren, Zhang, Kim, Liu, Wenger (Duke)
nodes.rationale: Submitted 2026-05-13, revised 2026-09-03 — one month before the event. It already does per-visitor minting, fingerprint-keyed identity (same User-Agent + ASN = same scraper), the scraper-to-token ledger, and mint-to-sighting resolution, across 22 production LLM systems, and it says its fingerprinting 'can be easily extended to use arbitrarily complex fingerprinting techniques, such as TLS fingerprinting'. The novel residue of Canary Maze is the sighting channel ONLY: an HTTP refetch by a different fingerprint instead of prompting a chatbot and waiting two months. Must be cited in the README and positioned against explicitly — an unacknowledged overlap reads far worse than the overlap itself.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 'false-positive rate bounded by HMAC collision' is falsified
nodes.source_location: section 2 — most likely reason it fails
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: The central claim is false as written. The HMAC bounds only whether the token is one you minted and which fingerprint it was minted for; it says nothing about whether two different fingerprints are two different actors. The inference 'minted for A, fetched by B therefore A and B talked' requires fingerprint A != fingerprint B implies actor A != actor B — a classifier assumption, precisely the assumption the idea claims to escape. Mandatory fix: render token authenticity as a solid edge and actor distinctness as a dashed one.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: one actor label carries 741 IPs across 114 /16s
nodes.source_location: section 2 — most likely reason it fails
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: Measured in the organizers' labels.jsonl.gz on 2026-10-02: a single actor label shows stored_revisions 899 against stored_revision_ips 741 and stored_revision_ip16 114. Every intra-actor fingerprint change in that corpus would register as a sighting — a propagation edge between an actor and itself — so the false-positive rate is bounded by nothing. This is the event's own reference data falsifying the HMAC claim.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 0 DOIs, 0 ISBNs, 0 cite templates across 14,591 revisions
nodes.source_location: section 3 — most likely reason it fails
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: Measured directly against the organizers' dump on 2026-10-02 by running C2's own extractors over all 14,591 revisions and 3,103 actor labels: DOI 0 (0.00%), ISBN 0, <ref>/{{cite}} 0, loosest journal-ish (YYYY) proxy 44 (0.30%), bare URL 10,101 (69.23%). Distinct DOIs in the entire corpus: zero. Three of the four extractors in the specification have nothing to extract, so the brief's hedge 'citation density there is probably low' was wrong in kind, not degree — a guess where a 4.2 MB download gives a number. Must never be reintroduced.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: 8,473 URLs shared by 2+ actors are shared tooling, not shared sources
nodes.source_location: section 3 — most likely reason it fails
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: 23,617 distinct URLs of which 8,473 are shared by two or more actors, with top hosts wikiservice.at 2,412, jqp.vercel.app 1,523, api.datausa.io 1,017, www.sec.gov 660, md.succ.ai 498, markdown.new 192, pure.md 145, r.jina.ai 109 — the wiki's own host plus URL-to-markdown scraping proxies and public data APIs. A join on shared URL yields thousands of groups all meaning 'two agents used the same scraper', so 'a fabricated citation is a near-perfect join key' is contradicted on the only corpus available: the identifier classes that would be near-perfect are empty and the populated class is saturated with trivial co-occurrence. Requiring k>=2 shared fabrications does not save it when top hosts are shared by hundreds.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: ~95% of the prt-scan campaign is a single account
nodes.source_location: section 4 — most likely reason it fails
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: The Wiz report checks out, but ezmtebo alone opened over 475 of the well-over-500 malicious PRs in 26 hours, so ~95% of the only cited campaign is one account — a shape a per-repo open-PR cap plus a rate limit already handles. The cross-account join, the part the cap provably cannot do, is the remaining ~25 PRs. The demo headline '14 of 112 opened by 9 accounts' would be generated almost entirely by the already-solved feature while the novel feature carries a tail. The omission of this distribution is itself the whole argument; find a batch where the cross-account join does the work.

nodes.label: KILL FACT: no maintainer asked for batch-identifying labels
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: GitHub community discussion #185387, running 2026-01-27 to 2026-08-04: blocking/banning and rate limits are most requested, cross-repo detection 'wasn't a common theme', 'No maintainers explicitly asked for batch-identifying labels', and the thread emphasises friction-adding mechanisms (issue-first workflows, CI gates, templates) over detection/attribution. One maintainer did say 'I had to batch-close several AI generated PRs which were all submitted around the same time' — real demand, but for batch CLOSING, not batch labelling. Corroborates the 2.1%-label / 20.8%-ban policy split. Fix: ship a blocklist export, bulk-close list, ruleset or abuse report instead.

nodes.label: GitHub post: how pull request limits are cutting down the noise
nodes.author: GitHub
nodes.rationale: Published 2026-06-18 (not the 17th as the brief claimed). The platform owner names C3's exact gap in writing: the cap 'does nothing when someone opens pull requests across hundreds of repositories at once', with trust signals, rate limiting and other cross-repository controls still only being explored. The single strongest fact in the whole candidate set, which the generating pass filed as counter-evidence — invert the pitch and lead with it. Also corroborates monthly PR volume rising from 25M (Jan 2023) to 90M (June 2026), and mentions PR archiving shipping soon plus issue limits in development.

nodes.label: Good Egg Trust Scoring action and Repository Policy Score
nodes.rationale: Named by maintainers in the GitHub community thread as already in use. Search-title-only leads not opened alongside them: ai-moderator, anti-slop, niubi_guard, pr-triage-web, Spamtoberfest.

nodes.label: links.jsonl.gz (collusion.wiki dump)
nodes.source_location: section 3 — the organizers already ship steps 1, 3 and 4
nodes.rationale: 23,877 rows, schema {url, host, record_ids, relation, followed, source_url_sha256, url_withheld}. record_ids is the inverted index from URL back to the revisions containing it and there is already a followed boolean — that is C2's extract-and-index step, pre-computed and published, and never flagged in the brief. The baseline a judge will name is one groupby away from the product.

nodes.label: Correction: SimilarEditors is archived, not paused
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: The quoted 'deployment is paused as of July 2023' is stale by three years. The page, last updated 2026-09-02, says the extension 'has not been maintained for some time, and no longer supports recent releases of MediaWiki. It was archived per T436880.' The correction favours the no-competitor claim, but quoting a 2023 status in an October 2026 write-up tells a jury the author did not re-check, which costs more than it gains.

nodes.label: Overclaim: resolution is not 'deterministic'
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: HTTP HEAD against the live web is not deterministic: Cloudflare 403s, paywalls, 429s, geo-blocks, link rot, robots refusals, and legitimate pre-DOI-era journals and offline books all return 'does not resolve'. Each one becomes a false fabrication claim fed into an accusation of sockpuppetry. Related: 'same hand OR same model' is not a mitigation but an admission that the join key does not identify an actor, and a group that might be one hand or two strangers using the same model is not actionable in an SPI filing.

nodes.label: Structural finding: C2 and C3 are the same mechanism
nodes.source_location: section 1 — overlap with the organizers' list
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: Both are 'group accounts by a shared deterministic artefact, then present the group' — one keyed on a fabricated citation, the other on a near-duplicate PR body. They differ in venue and key, not in mechanism, and both are coordinated-inauthentic-behaviour detection, a pre-registered recycled shape. C1 is the only genuinely different idea in the set and the only one that is neither a classifier nor a clusterer, though it lands on two organizer suggestions at once (#5 information spread, #6 web/digital forensics), so the write-up should not claim distance it does not have.

nodes.label: Theme-fit risk ranking (C3 worst, then C2, then C1)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: C2 is honest in name but off-theme in execution: the agent wiki is genuinely agents (3,103 labels, is_human_handle False, names like A3ReadOnlyForensics, AICountyResearch, AgentDataUSAProbeFebX2), but C2 cannot run there, so the honest venue and the workable venue are different wikis. C3 is the biggest off-brief exposure: prt-scan is one human running six accounts with automation, not agents coordinating with each other, and the surrounding ~17M AI-authored PRs/month flood is uncoordinated. C1 is on-theme but its expected first result (GPTBot crawls, ChatGPT-User fetches) is one company's two services sharing a database — a true result about infrastructure and a null result about swarms. None is disqualifying if the write-up is honest; all three become disqualifying if 'swarm' papers over the gap, because this jury wrote the brief and will test the word.

nodes.label: Build the result, do not wait for it (seeded replay plus triggered sighting)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: If the sighting never fires, what is left is the Duke paper's setup with none of its results, and 'deployed, not fired yet' is the one project that cannot afford the optional real-results section to be empty, because its whole pitch is manufacturing evidence rather than inferring it. Two schedulable moves: a labelled synthetic replay as the primary deliverable alongside an honest live log ('0 organic sightings in 31 hours'), and pasting a minted URL into three public AI chat products to watch which fetchers come back — repeatable within 20 hours, with the honest caveat that it shows 'a product's fetcher followed a human's paste', not 'agents talked'.

nodes.label: What eats the weekend, per idea (DNS, the resolver, the GH Archive replay)
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: C1: the serving layer and an unbounded per-visitor URL space that must stay stable long enough to be refetched — the glamour is in the graph but the weekend goes to DNS, TLS, sitemap and forking an unfamiliar 125-star repo. C2: four independent resolution paths whose failure mode IS the product's positive signal, so every unhandled false negative becomes a published fabricated-source claim about a named account. C3: the GH Archive replay of 24 days of hourly archives plus a GitHub App that is a second full build whose cross-install index will have exactly one install — two weekends, and the App is the cuttable half because the public events API gives the cross-repo profile without any install.

nodes.label: Leninist historiography case (AI-written article with fake sources)
nodes.rationale: Documented real case held by the community that owns the problem: an article 'entirely written by AI' that 'included a list of completely fake sources in Russian and Hungarian at the bottom of the page. Google turned up no results for these sources.' Evidence the pain is real even though WikiProject AI Cleanup treats AI misuse as individual editors needing education rather than as coordination.

nodes.label: arXiv:2605.08583 — Source or It Didn't Happen (multi-agent citation hallucination detection)
nodes.rationale: Title only — a LEAD. Listed alongside commercial leads AiCitationChecker, Sourcely Citation Verifier and Citely, which together make the resolution half of C2 a commodity.

nodes.label: Interesting-but-not-good: novelty with no reachable pain
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: C2's join key really is absent from every grouping tool opened, so it is novel — and there is no evidence anyone has the pain in a form the key can reach: zero DOIs in the event corpus, and the community that owns the problem does not frame it as coordination at all. Novelty with no reachable pain is the definition of interesting-but-not-good. The salvage is the pre-filled investigation-page output format, moved inside another idea.

nodes.label: Reduction test: all three candidates have model-free deterministic cores
nodes.author: Subagent K
nodes.rationale: None of the three is a model wrapper: HMAC mint plus fingerprint ledger, DOI/ISBN/HTTP resolution, and minhash plus LSH over text are classic model-free computer science that would still run if every LLM vanished. C1 is the cleanest pass (no model anywhere on the primary path; only the paraphrase-matching side table dies, and it is already quarantined out of the proof graph). C2 is substantial on the reduction axis and dies on data instead. C3's reduction - a PR title and body to a minhash, out comes a batch id - is 1990s computer science and survives. This is the one thing the generating pass got right.
